sentences.text: Nigersaurus was a relatively small sauropod, reaching lengths of 9 to 14.1 meters and weighing between 1.9 and 4 metric tons, a size comparable to a modern elephant.

It possessed a wide muzzle packed with over 500 teeth that were replaced roughly every 14 days, and its jaw bones were rotated transversely so all teeth faced forward, a unique arrangement among tetrapods.
Despite having a brain size similar to other dinosaurs, the animal had an underdeveloped olfactory region and lacked an advanced sense of smell.
Its eyes were positioned high on the skull above the muzzle, creating overlapping fields of view.
The species was discovered in the Elrhaz Formation at Gadoufaoua in Niger, and the specific name taqueti honors Philippe Taquet, who found the initial remains.

Although fossils were first described in 1976, the species was not formally named until 1999, remaining poorly known until Paul Sereno led expeditions in 1997 and 2000 that uncovered additional material.
This dinosaur inhabited a riparian environment and likely consumed soft vegetation such as ferns, horsetails, and early flowering plants.
In 1999, Sereno and colleagues classified Nigersaurus as a rebbachisaurid diplodocoid within the subfamily Rebbachisaurinae.
John A. Whitlock named the subfamily Nigersaurinae in 2011 to include Nigersaurus and related genera, though a 2015 study suggested this group might be a junior synonym of Rebbachisaurinae.
Nigersaurus lived in what is now Africa during the mid-Cretaceous period, specifically between 121.4 and 100.5 million years ago, spanning the Aptian to Albian ages.

Scientists debate whether Nigersaurus habitually held its head downwards or horizontally like other sauropods, with a 2020 study cautioning against using semicircular canals to infer precise skull orientation due to discrepancies in resting poses.
It is also debated whether the clade Rebbachisaurinae necessarily includes Nigersaurus, as some studies place it as a sister taxon to other nigersaurines.
